newsitem.title: USA: Gore's Asia trip ends with mixed assessments.
newsitem.headline: Gore's Asia trip ends with mixed assessments.

text.p: Depending on who your sources are, Vice President Al Gore's eight-day trip to Japan, China and South Korea was a brilliant success, a serious disappointment or a confusing mix of both.
The mixed signals were not what Gore, a man who harbors dreams of becoming president, had in mind when he set out on one of the highest-profile assignments of his vice presidency.
"I think the mission was accomplished," an upbeat Gore, who celebrates his 49th birthday on Monday, said as he returned to Washington late on Saturday to end his first trip to Asia as vice president.
He was the highest-ranking American to visit Beijing since China's government shocked the world by ordering its troops to crush pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in 1989.

One of those with whom he met was Premier Li Peng, called the "Butcher of Beijing" by some in the West for his role in the Tiananmen massacre. In one particularly awkward moment, Gore found himself publicly clicking champagne glasses with Li at the signing of major business deals with Boeing and GM.

While human rights activists were upset about the meeting with Li, Gore was carrying out a U.S. policy of active engagement with China as it prepares to take control of Hong Kong in July and seeks a bigger role on the economic stage.

"We made tremendous progress in lending forward momentum in our relations with China," Gore said. "It is obvious in the aftermath of the visit there that the Chinese feel as we do that we have new momentum."

But much of the substance of his five-day visit to China was overshadowed by allegations before he left home that Beijing had illegally tried to tamper with 1996 U.S. elections by funneling cash to political candidates -- a controversey that keeps alive questions about Gore's problems with a visit last year to a Buddhist temple fundraiser.

Gore and his advisers are frustrated by what they consider unfair criticism of his China trip, which some have cast as a poorly handled diplomatic mission that left the vice president returning home empty-handed.

Although the Chinese have a reputation as tough negotiators unwilling to make concessions, there had been speculation they might at least make some gesture in response to Gore's visit -- like freeing one or more of the dissidents he voiced concerns about in private.

Gore's aides argue that the trip was never intended to be a showcase of personal triumph for him but was an effort to lay the groundwork for a scheduled summit late in the year in Washington between President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
In the world of diplomacy and politics, there is one simple rule -- the boss gets the credit, not the chief assistant.

Unlike most previous vice presidents, who used their overseas excursions as a way of proving their relevance and improving their stature, Gore went to Asia with his credentials well established as a force in the Clinton Administration. But that background makes it more difficult for him to fulfill the traditional role he must serve as a vice president -- making certain the president gets the glory.

Clinton, who says he has run his final campaign for office, has gone from thinking about facing voters in the next election to worrying about the next generation of historians and what their opinions of him will be.
With a Republican-controlled Congress limiting his chances for shaping landmark domestic changes, foreign policy poses the best opportunity for Clinton to leave a mark.

For Gore, the task is to serve his president and himself, something that will be increasingly difficult as likely challengers for the Democratic Party presidential nomination in 2000 become more active.

While Gore was in Asia, one of those prospective challengers, House of Representatives Democratic Leader Richard Gephart, was in Iowa and New Hampshire, the first two hurdles in the 2000 race, sending a clear signal that Gore is not alone in dreaming about the White House.
